words.w: What happens when you open a URL?
words.t: First the browser uses DNS to turn the domain name into an IP address. Then it opens a connection to the server, and for HTTPS it does a TLS handshake to make the connection secure. It sends an HTTP request and gets HTML back. The browser builds the DOM from the HTML and the CSSOM from the CSS, and puts them together into a render tree. Then it calculates layout (sizes and positions), paints the pixels, and shows the page. Scripts without async or defer can block this process.
a: What happens when you open a URL

words.w: async vs defer on a script tag?
words.t: Both attributes load the script in the background, so the page does not stop while the file downloads. The difference is when the script runs. With defer, the script runs after the HTML is fully parsed, and scripts run in the same order as in the page. With async, the script runs as soon as it is loaded, so the order is not guaranteed. I use defer for my app code and async for independent scripts like analytics.
a: async vs defer on a script tag

words.w: Why do semantic HTML and accessibility matter?
words.t: Semantic HTML means using tags for their meaning: button for actions, nav for navigation, label for form fields, h1 to h6 for headings. Screen readers use these tags to explain the page to blind users. Search engines also understand the page better, which helps SEO. Native elements give keyboard support for free: a real button works with Tab and Enter, a div does not. I also add alt text to images, connect labels to inputs, and move focus into a modal and back when it closes.
a: Why do semantic HTML and accessibility matter

words.w: Reflow vs repaint?
words.t: Reflow, or layout, is when the browser calculates the size and position of elements again. It happens when I change width, height, margins, add elements, or change the text. It is expensive, because one change can move many other elements. Repaint only draws pixels again, for example when the color changes, and it is cheaper. For animations I use transform and opacity, because they skip both reflow and repaint and run on the GPU.
a: Reflow vs repaint

words.w: localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies vs IndexedDB?
words.t: localStorage keeps data until you delete it, about 5 MB, and it is shared between tabs of the same site. sessionStorage works the same way, but the data lives only in one tab and is gone when the tab closes. Cookies are small, about 4 KB, and the browser sends them to the server with every request, so they are used for sessions. IndexedDB is a real database in the browser for large data and offline apps, and its API is async. I never keep tokens in localStorage, because any injected script can read it.
a: localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies vs IndexedDB

words.w: Explain the box model.
words.t: Every element is a box with four layers: content in the middle, then padding, then border, then margin outside. By default, box-sizing is content-box, so width is only the content, and padding and border are added on top. With box-sizing: border-box, width includes padding and border, so the size is easier to control. Most projects set border-box for all elements. Also, vertical margins of two blocks can collapse into one margin.
a: Explain the box model

words.w: How does CSS specificity work?
words.t: When two CSS rules set the same property, the browser chooses the more specific selector. Inline styles are the strongest, then IDs, then classes, attributes and pseudo-classes, then tags. If the specificity is the same, the rule that comes later wins. !important beats everything, but it makes code hard to maintain, so I avoid it. In practice I keep specificity low and flat, for example one class per element, like in BEM or CSS Modules.
a: How does CSS specificity work

words.w: Flexbox vs Grid?
words.t: Flexbox works in one direction: a row or a column. It is great for aligning items inside a component, for example a navbar, a button with an icon, or centering something. Grid works in two directions at once: rows and columns. It is great for page layouts and card grids, where items must line up in both directions. Often I use Grid for the page structure and Flexbox inside the components. Both use gap for spacing between items.
a: Flexbox vs Grid

words.w: What are the CSS position values?
words.t: position controls two things: does the element stay in the normal flow, and what is it placed against. static is the default: the element is in the normal flow, and top or left do nothing. relative keeps the element's space but lets me move it a little with top and left; it also becomes the anchor for absolute children. absolute takes the element out of the flow and places it against the nearest parent that is not static. fixed is placed against the screen, so it does not move when you scroll. sticky works like relative until you scroll to a point, for example top: 0, and then it sticks inside its parent.
a: What are the CSS position values

words.w: Why doesn't my z-index work?
words.t: z-index only works on positioned elements (not static) and on flex or grid children. It also only compares elements inside the same stacking context. A new stacking context is created by a parent with position and z-index, or with transform, opacity less than 1, or filter. So a child with z-index 9999 still cannot go above an element outside its parent's context. To fix it, I find the parent that creates the context, or I render the dropdown or modal in a portal at the end of body.
a: Why doesn't my z-index work

words.w: How do you build a responsive layout?
words.t: I start mobile-first: base styles for small screens, then min-width media queries add changes for bigger screens. I use flexible units like rem, % and fr instead of fixed pixels. Flexbox and Grid with auto-fit and minmax let the layout adapt without many breakpoints. Images use srcset and sizes, so phones download smaller files. I also add the viewport meta tag and test on real devices. For components, container queries let them adapt to the size of their container, not the whole window.
a: How do you build a responsive layout

words.w: BEM vs CSS Modules vs CSS-in-JS vs Tailwind?
words.t: All four solve one problem: CSS is global, so styles can leak and break other parts of the page. BEM is a naming rule, like block__element--modifier, so it needs discipline but no tools. CSS Modules make class names unique automatically for each file. CSS-in-JS, like styled-components, writes styles in JavaScript and can use props, but runtime versions are slower and do not work well with Server Components. Tailwind gives small utility classes in the markup, so CSS stays small and there are no naming problems. Today I usually pick CSS Modules or Tailwind.
a: BEM vs CSS Modules vs CSS-in-JS vs Tailwind

words.w: What are the data types? == vs ===?
words.t: JavaScript has 7 primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol. Everything else is an object, including arrays and functions. Primitives are compared by value, objects by reference. === checks value and type without converting anything. == converts types first, so 0 == '' and null == undefined are true, which causes bugs. I always use ===. Also note that typeof null is 'object', which is an old bug in the language.
a: What are the data types? == vs ===

words.w: var vs let vs const and hoisting?
words.t: var is function-scoped, so it is visible in the whole function, even outside the block where it was declared. let and const are block-scoped, so they live only inside the curly braces. All of them are hoisted, which means the engine knows about them before the code runs. But var starts as undefined, and let and const are in the temporal dead zone: reading them before the declaration throws an error. const means the variable cannot be reassigned, but an object inside it can still change. I use const by default, let when I need to reassign, and never var.
a: var vs let vs const and hoisting

words.w: What is a closure?
words.t: A closure is a function together with the variables around it. When I create a function inside another function, the inner function remembers the outer variables, even after the outer function has finished. I use closures to keep private data, for example a counter that nobody can change from outside. Debounce, event handlers and all React hooks work because of closures. A common bug is a stale closure: a callback keeps an old value from the moment it was created.
a: What is a closure

words.w: How is "this" determined?
words.t: For a normal function, this depends on how the function is called, not where it is written. If I call obj.method(), this is obj. If I call the function alone, this is undefined in strict mode. With call, apply or bind, I choose this myself, and with new, this is the new object. Arrow functions are different: they do not have their own this, they take it from the code around them. That is why arrow functions are good for callbacks inside class methods.
a: How is "this" determined

words.w: How do prototypes and classes work?
words.t: Every object has a hidden link to another object, its prototype. When I read a property that the object does not have, JavaScript looks in the prototype, then in the prototype's prototype, and so on. This is the prototype chain, and it ends with null. Methods live on the prototype, so all objects share one copy. Classes are just nicer syntax over this: class methods go to the prototype, and extends connects two prototypes. So a class in JavaScript is still a function with a prototype.
a: How do prototypes and classes work

words.w: Explain the event loop.
words.t: JavaScript runs on one thread, so the event loop decides what runs next. First, all synchronous code on the call stack runs. When the stack is empty, the loop runs all microtasks: promise callbacks and code after await. Then it takes one macrotask, for example a setTimeout callback or a click event. Between tasks the browser can render the page. That is why a promise callback always runs before setTimeout with zero delay, and why a long loop freezes the page.
a: Explain the event loop

words.w: Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any?
words.t: All four take an array of promises and run them in parallel. Promise.all waits for all of them and gives an array of results, but fails as soon as one promise fails. Promise.allSettled waits for all of them and never fails; it gives the status and result of each one. Promise.race finishes with the first promise that settles, success or error, so it is useful for timeouts. Promise.any finishes with the first success and fails only if all of them fail. I use all when I need every result, and allSettled when some requests may fail.
a: Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any

words.w: Debounce vs throttle?
words.t: Both limit how often a function runs when an event fires many times. Debounce waits until the events stop for some time, for example 300 ms, and then runs the function once. It is good for a search input: we send one request after the user stops typing. Throttle runs the function at most once per time period, for example once every 100 ms, while the events continue. It is good for scroll and resize handlers. Both are built with setTimeout and a closure.
a: Debounce vs throttle

words.w: What are event bubbling and delegation?
words.t: When I click an element, the event first goes down from the window to the element (capturing), and then goes back up through all parents (bubbling). Most handlers listen during bubbling. Delegation uses this: I put one listener on a parent and check event.target to see which child was clicked. This is useful for long lists or items added later, because I need only one listener. stopPropagation stops the event from going further up, but I use it carefully because it can break other handlers.
a: What are event bubbling and delegation

words.w: Shallow vs deep copy?
words.t: A shallow copy creates a new object, but nested objects are still shared with the original. Spread syntax and Object.assign make shallow copies. So if I change a nested field in the copy, the original changes too. A deep copy duplicates everything, at every level. The modern way is structuredClone, which also works with Dates, Maps and circular links. The JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) trick is older and loses undefined, functions and Dates. In React I usually copy only the parts I change.
a: Shallow vs deep copy

words.w: ES modules vs CommonJS, and what is tree shaking?
words.t: CommonJS is the old Node.js system: require() and module.exports. It loads files at runtime, one by one, and require can be called anywhere, even inside an if. ES modules use import and export, which are static: they must be at the top level, so tools know all imports before the code runs. Because of this, a bundler can see which exports are never used and remove them from the bundle. That is tree shaking. It works only with ES modules and with code that has no side effects on import.
a: ES modules vs CommonJS, and what is tree shaking

words.w: interface vs type?
words.t: Both describe the shape of an object, and in most cases they work the same. An interface can be extended with extends, and two interfaces with the same name merge into one, which is useful for adding fields to library types. A type alias can describe more things: unions, tuples, function types, mapped and conditional types. A type cannot be declared twice. Many teams use interface for objects and component props, and type for unions and more complex types. The important thing is to be consistent in the project.
a: interface vs type

words.w: any vs unknown vs never?
words.t: any turns type checking off: you can do anything with the value, and errors appear only at runtime. unknown is the safe version: you can store any value, but you must check its type before you use it, for example with typeof or a schema. I use unknown for data from outside, like API responses or JSON.parse. never means a value that can never exist, for example the return type of a function that always throws. It is also used to check that a switch handles every case of a union.
a: any vs unknown vs never

words.w: What are generics?
words.t: Generics are type parameters, like arguments but for types. They let one function or component work with many types and still keep the exact type. For example, function first<T>(arr: T[]): T returns a number for a number array and a string for a string array. Without generics I would need any and would lose type safety. I can limit a generic with extends, for example T extends { id: string }. In React I use generics for things like a typed Table or Select component.
a: What are generics

words.w: Which utility types do you use?
words.t: Utility types are built-in helpers that create a new type from an existing one. Partial makes all fields optional, which is useful for update forms. Required makes all fields required. Pick takes only some fields, and Omit removes some fields, for example Omit<User, 'password'>. Record<K, V> describes an object with known key and value types. ReturnType and Parameters take types from a function, and Awaited takes the value from a promise. They help me avoid writing the same type twice.
a: Which utility types do you use

words.w: What are narrowing and discriminated unions?
words.t: Narrowing means that after a check, TypeScript knows a more exact type. For example, after if (typeof x === 'string') TypeScript treats x as a string inside that block. It also works with in, instanceof, null checks and my own type guard functions. A discriminated union is a union where every variant has a common field with a unique value, like status: 'loading' | 'success' | 'error'. When I check status, TypeScript knows which other fields exist. It is perfect for API states and reducer actions.
a: What are narrowing and discriminated unions

words.w: What do ^ and ~ mean, and why a lock file?
words.t: In package.json, ^1.2.3 allows minor and patch updates, so 1.x.x. ~1.2.3 allows only patch updates, so 1.2.x. That means two developers can install different versions from the same package.json. The lock file (package-lock.json or yarn.lock) saves the exact version of every package, including dependencies of dependencies. So everyone, and the CI server, installs exactly the same code. I always commit the lock file and use npm ci in CI.
a: What do ^ and ~ mean, and why a lock file

words.w: What does a bundler do? Why is Vite fast?
words.t: A bundler takes many source files and their imports and builds a few optimized files for the browser. On the way it compiles TypeScript and JSX, minifies the code, removes unused code with tree shaking, and splits the code into chunks. Webpack bundles everything even in development, so it gets slow on big projects. Vite in development does not bundle: it gives the browser native ES modules and compiles only the files that are requested, using esbuild. That is why it starts fast and updates fast. For production Vite builds a normal optimized bundle.
a: What does a bundler do? Why is Vite fast

words.w: git merge vs rebase?
words.t: Both bring changes from one branch into another. Merge creates a merge commit and keeps the history exactly as it happened, with all branches. Rebase moves my commits on top of the other branch, so the history becomes one straight line. Rebase gives a cleaner history, but it rewrites commits, so their hashes change. The rule: never rebase a branch that other people already use. I rebase my own feature branch on main, and merge into main with a pull request.
a: git merge vs rebase

words.w: When does a React component re-render?
words.t: A component re-renders in three cases: its own state changes, its parent re-renders, or a context it uses changes. Props changing is not a separate reason: props change because the parent re-rendered. By default, when a parent re-renders, all its children re-render too, even if their props are the same. A re-render does not always mean a DOM update; React updates the DOM only where the result is different. If renders are slow, I move state down, or use React.memo with stable props.
a: When does a React component re-render

words.w: What are the virtual DOM, reconciliation and Fiber?
words.t: The virtual DOM is a light JavaScript description of the UI that components return. When state changes, React creates a new description and compares it with the old one. This comparison is reconciliation. Then React changes only the real DOM nodes that are different, because DOM changes are expensive. Fiber is the engine inside React since version 16. It splits rendering into small units of work, so React can pause, give priority to urgent updates like typing, and continue later.
a: What are the virtual DOM, reconciliation and Fiber

words.w: Why are keys important? Why not the index?
words.t: When React renders a list, keys tell it which item is which between renders. With stable keys, React can move, add or remove only the changed items, and each item keeps its own state. If I use the array index and an item is added at the start, removed or sorted, the indexes move to other items. Then React mixes up the state, for example an input shows text from another row. So I use a stable id from the data. The index is fine only for static lists that never change.
a: Why are keys important? Why not the index

words.w: What are the rules of hooks?
words.t: There are two rules. First, call hooks only at the top level of a component, not inside if, loops or nested functions. Second, call hooks only from React components or from custom hooks. The reason is that React does not know hooks by name; it remembers them by their order in every render. If a hook is skipped in one render, the order breaks and the state goes to the wrong hook. The ESLint plugin for hooks checks these rules for me.
a: What are the rules of hooks

words.w: How does useEffect work?
words.t: useEffect connects a component to something outside React: a subscription, a timer, a request, or a browser API. The effect runs after React updates the screen. The dependency array decides when it runs again: an empty array means only after the first render, and with values it runs again when one of them changes. The function returned from the effect is cleanup: React calls it before the next run and when the component unmounts. I use cleanup to remove listeners, clear timers and cancel requests. If a value can be calculated during render, I do not need an effect.
a: How does useEffect work

words.w: What is a stale closure in React?
words.t: Every render creates new functions, and each function remembers the values from its own render. A stale closure is when a callback or an effect still uses old values from an earlier render. A classic example is setInterval in useEffect with an empty dependency array: it always sees count = 0. To fix it, I add the value to the dependencies, or use the function form of setState like setCount(c => c + 1). Another fix is to keep the latest value in a ref.
a: What is a stale closure in React

words.w: useMemo vs useCallback vs React.memo?
words.t: All three help to skip unnecessary work. React.memo wraps a component and skips its re-render if the props did not change. useCallback keeps the same function between renders, and useMemo keeps the result of a calculation. They are often used together: a memo child gets a function from useCallback, otherwise the new function on every render breaks memo. useMemo is for expensive calculations or for objects passed as props. They are not free, so I use them when the Profiler shows a real problem.
a: useMemo vs useCallback vs React.memo

words.w: What is useRef for?
words.t: useRef gives an object with a current field that stays the same between renders. Changing ref.current does not cause a re-render. The first use is access to a DOM element: I pass the ref to an element and then call focus() or measure its size. The second use is to keep any value that must survive renders but is not shown on the screen, for example a timer id, the previous value, or the latest callback. If the value must update the UI, I use state instead.
a: What is useRef for

words.w: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect?
words.t: Both run after React updates the DOM, but at different moments. useLayoutEffect runs before the browser paints the screen, and it blocks painting until it finishes. useEffect runs after the paint, so it does not block the user. I use useLayoutEffect only when I need to measure the DOM and change something before the user sees it, for example the position of a tooltip, to avoid flicker. For everything else, like requests and subscriptions, I use useEffect.
a: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect

words.w: When useReducer instead of useState?
words.t: useReducer is better when the state has several values that change together, or when the next state depends on complex rules. All update logic goes into one reducer function: it takes the current state and an action and returns the new state. This makes the logic easy to read and easy to test without React. Components only dispatch actions like { type: 'added' }. dispatch is stable, so it is easy to pass down. For one or two simple values, useState is enough.
a: When useReducer instead of useState

words.w: Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs?
words.t: A controlled input gets its value from React state and updates the state in onChange. React is the single source of truth, so I can validate, format or block input on every key press. The cost is a re-render on every key press. An uncontrolled input keeps its value in the DOM, and I read it with a ref or from the form when it is submitted. It is simpler and faster for big forms. Libraries like React Hook Form use uncontrolled inputs for this reason.
a: Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs

words.w: What's the performance problem with Context?
words.t: When a context value changes, every component that uses this context re-renders, even if it needs only a small part of the value. A common mistake is to pass a new object as the value on every render, so all consumers re-render every time. To fix it, I wrap the value in useMemo, split one big context into smaller ones by how often they change, and put setters in a separate context. Context has no selectors. For state that changes often, a store like Zustand or Redux is better.
a: What's the performance problem with Context

words.w: What is a custom hook?
words.t: A custom hook is a normal function whose name starts with use and which calls other hooks. It lets me move logic out of a component and reuse it in many components, for example useFetch, useDebounce or useLocalStorage. Each component that calls the hook gets its own separate state; the hook shares logic, not data. The use prefix tells React and the linter to check the rules of hooks. Custom hooks also make components shorter and easier to test.
a: What is a custom hook

words.w: What are Error Boundaries?
words.t: An error boundary is a component that catches errors during rendering in its children and shows a fallback UI instead of a white screen. It also logs the error, for example to Sentry. It is written as a class with getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch, or with a library like react-error-boundary. It does not catch errors in event handlers, in async code like setTimeout or fetch, or in the boundary itself. I put boundaries around independent parts of the page, so one broken widget does not break the whole app.
a: What are Error Boundaries

words.w: What are Suspense, lazy and portals for?
words.t: React.lazy loads a component's code only when it is first rendered, so the main bundle is smaller. I use it for pages and heavy widgets like charts or editors. Suspense shows a fallback, like a spinner or a skeleton, while that code or data is loading. One Suspense can wait for several lazy parts at once. A portal renders a component into another DOM node, usually the end of body. It is used for modals, tooltips and dropdowns, so overflow: hidden and z-index of parents do not cut them. Events and context still work as if the portal were inside its React parent.
a: What are Suspense, lazy and portals for

words.w: What changed in React 18 and 19?
words.t: React 18 added concurrent rendering: React can pause a big render and handle urgent updates, like typing, first. With it came useTransition and useDeferredValue to mark updates as not urgent, and automatic batching of all state updates, even in promises and timers. It also added streaming server rendering with Suspense. React 19 made async work and forms simpler: actions, useActionState, useOptimistic, and the use hook for reading promises and context. In React 19, ref is a normal prop, so forwardRef is not needed. Server Components became stable too.
a: What changed in React 18 and 19

words.w: What are React Server Components?
words.t: Server Components run only on the server, for example during the build or on each request. They can read a database or files directly, and their code is never sent to the browser, so the bundle is smaller. They cannot use state, effects or event handlers. For interactive parts I write Client Components and mark the file with 'use client'. A Server Component can render Client Components and pass them serializable props. In Next.js App Router, all components are Server Components by default.
a: What are React Server Components

words.w: Where should state live?
words.t: I choose the place by the type of state. Data from the server goes into a query library like TanStack Query, which handles caching, loading and refetching. Local UI state, like an open modal or an input value, stays in useState in the component that needs it. State shared by many components, like the current user or a cart, goes into context or a small store like Zustand or Redux. Filters, sorting and the current page go into the URL, so the user can refresh or share the link. Values that can be calculated are not stored at all.
a: Where should state live

words.w: What is Redux and what does Redux Toolkit improve?
words.t: Redux keeps the whole app state in one store. The only way to change it is to dispatch an action, and a pure reducer function returns the new state. This makes changes predictable and easy to debug with Redux DevTools and time travel. Classic Redux needed a lot of code: action types, action creators, switch statements and immutable updates. Redux Toolkit removes most of it: createSlice makes actions and reducers together, Immer lets me write simple mutating code safely, and configureStore sets up good defaults. RTK Query also adds data fetching and caching.
a: What is Redux and what does Redux Toolkit improve

words.w: TanStack Query vs Zustand vs Redux Toolkit?
words.t: They solve different problems. TanStack Query manages server state: it fetches data, caches it by key, shows loading and error states, refetches in the background, and handles mutations. Zustand is a small store for client state, with almost no code and no provider; components subscribe with selectors. Redux Toolkit also manages client state, but with more structure, middleware and great dev tools, which helps big teams. Often a project uses TanStack Query for API data plus Zustand or Redux for UI state.
a: TanStack Query vs Zustand vs Redux Toolkit

words.w: What does stale-while-revalidate mean?
words.t: Stale-while-revalidate is a caching strategy. When the user needs data, we show the cached copy right away, even if it may be old. At the same time we send a request in the background to get fresh data. When the new data arrives, the cache and the UI update. The user sees content immediately and gets fresh data a moment later. It is used in the Cache-Control header, in service workers, and in libraries like SWR and TanStack Query.
a: What does stale-while-revalidate mean

words.w: CSR vs SSR vs SSG vs ISR?
words.t: The difference is where and when the HTML is created. CSR: the server sends an almost empty page, and JavaScript builds everything in the browser, so the first load is slow and SEO is weak. SSR: the server builds the HTML on every request, so the page appears fast and is good for SEO, but the server works more. SSG: the HTML is built once at build time and served from a CDN, which is the fastest, but the data can be old. ISR is SSG plus a refresh: the page is rebuilt in the background after some time. I choose by how often the data changes and whether SEO matters.
a: CSR vs SSR vs SSG vs ISR

words.w: What is hydration?
words.t: With server rendering, the browser first gets ready HTML, so the user sees the page quickly, but buttons do not work yet. Hydration is when React loads in the browser, renders the same components again, and attaches event handlers to the existing HTML instead of creating it again. After that the page is interactive. The first render on the client must give the same result as on the server. If not, there is a hydration mismatch, for example when I use Date.now() or window during render.
a: What is hydration

words.w: What are the key ideas of the App Router?
words.t: In the App Router, folders inside the app directory are routes, and a page.tsx file makes the route visible. layout.tsx wraps pages and keeps its state when the user navigates between them. loading.tsx and error.tsx add Suspense and error boundaries for a route automatically. All components are Server Components by default, so they can fetch data directly with async and await, and I add 'use client' only for interactive parts. Server Actions let forms call server code without writing API routes. Next.js also caches fetch results and pages.
a: What are the key ideas of the App Router

words.w: What are Core Web Vitals?
words.t: Core Web Vitals are three Google metrics about real user experience. LCP, Largest Contentful Paint, is how fast the main content appears; a good value is 2.5 seconds or less. INP, Interaction to Next Paint, is how fast the page reacts to clicks and typing; good is 200 ms or less. CLS, Cumulative Layout Shift, is how much the layout jumps while loading; good is 0.1 or less. They affect SEO. I measure them with Lighthouse and with real user data, for example the web-vitals library.
a: What are Core Web Vitals

words.w: How do you make an app load faster?
words.t: First I measure with Lighthouse and the Network and Performance panels, to find the real problem. Then I send less code: code splitting by routes, lazy loading heavy components, removing big or unused libraries. I optimize images: modern formats like WebP or AVIF, the right size with srcset, and lazy loading below the fold. I use caching: a CDN, long cache for files with a hash in the name, and preload for critical resources like fonts. For content pages, SSR or SSG shows the HTML sooner. After each change I measure again.
a: How do you make an app load faster

words.w: How do you render a list of 10,000 items?
words.t: Rendering 10,000 DOM nodes at once is slow and uses a lot of memory. The main solution is virtualization: I render only the rows the user can see, plus a small buffer, and replace them while the user scrolls. Libraries like TanStack Virtual or react-window do this. Another option is pagination or infinite scroll, so I load and show data in parts. I also give each row a stable key and memoize rows, so one change does not re-render the whole list. For heavy filtering or sorting I use useMemo or a Web Worker.
a: How do you render a list of 10,000 items

words.w: What is XSS and how do you prevent it in React?
words.t: XSS, cross-site scripting, is when an attacker gets their JavaScript to run on my page, for example through a comment field. The script can steal data or act as the user. React protects by default: it escapes all text in JSX, so a script tag in the data is shown as text. The risky places are dangerouslySetInnerHTML, links with javascript: URLs, and direct DOM changes. If I must show user HTML, I clean it with DOMPurify first. A Content Security Policy and HttpOnly cookies add more protection.
a: What is XSS and how do you prevent it in React

words.w: What is CSRF?
words.t: CSRF, cross-site request forgery, works like this: the user is logged in to my site, then opens a bad site. The bad site sends a request to my server, for example a form that transfers money, and the browser automatically adds my site's cookies. So the server thinks the user made the request. To protect, I set cookies with SameSite=Lax or Strict, so the browser does not send them with cross-site requests. I also use CSRF tokens for forms and check the Origin header. Tokens in an Authorization header are not sent automatically, so they are not affected.
a: What is CSRF

words.w: What is the idea of React Testing Library?
words.t: The main idea of React Testing Library is to test the component the way a user uses it, not its internal details. I find elements by what the user sees: role, label or text, for example getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }). I interact with user-event, like clicking and typing, and then check the result on the screen. I do not check state, props or internal methods. So when I refactor the code but the behavior stays the same, the tests still pass. Searching by role also checks basic accessibility.
a: What is the idea of React Testing Library

words.w: getBy vs queryBy vs findBy?
words.t: They differ in what happens when the element is not there. getBy returns the element or throws an error immediately, so I use it when the element must be on the screen now. queryBy returns null instead of throwing, so I use it to check that something is not on the screen. findBy returns a promise and waits until the element appears, by default up to 1 second, so I use it for async content, like data after a request. Each one also has an AllBy version for many elements.
a: getBy vs queryBy vs findBy

words.w: What does the frontend testing pyramid look like?
words.t: The pyramid shows how many tests of each kind to write. At the bottom are many unit tests for pure functions, hooks and reducers; they are fast and cheap. In the middle are component and integration tests with React Testing Library, often with the network mocked by MSW; they check how parts work together. At the top are a few end-to-end tests with Playwright or Cypress that run the real app in a browser, for key flows like login and checkout. They are slow and can be flaky, so there are only a few. Many frontend teams put most tests in the middle layer.
a: What does the frontend testing pyramid look like

words.w: A form re-renders the whole page on every keystroke. What do you do?
words.t: First I measure with the React Profiler to see which components re-render and how long it takes. Usually the form state sits too high, for example in a page component, so every key press re-renders everything. I move the state down into the form or into each field. For big forms I use uncontrolled inputs with React Hook Form, so typing does not re-render the form at all. I also wrap heavy neighbor components in React.memo with stable props, and debounce expensive work like validation or search.
a: form re-renders the whole page on every keystroke. What do you do?

words.w: Search sometimes shows results for an old query. Why?
words.t: This is a race condition. The user types fast, so several requests are sent. If an older request is slower, its response arrives last and replaces the newer results. To fix it, I cancel the old request with AbortController in the useEffect cleanup, or ignore responses that do not match the current query. A library like TanStack Query solves it with a query key per search text. I also add a debounce of about 300 ms, so fewer requests are sent.
a: Search sometimes shows results for an old query. Why

words.w: Users double-click "Pay" and get two orders. How do you fix it?
words.t: On the frontend, I disable the button and show a spinner while the request is pending, and I ignore new clicks until it finishes. But this is not enough: the user can have a slow network, open two tabs, or the request can be retried. The real fix is on the backend: an idempotency key. The client creates a unique key for each payment and sends it with the request. If the server sees the same key again, it returns the first result instead of creating a second order.
a: Users double-click "Pay" and get two orders. How do you fix it

words.w: The bundle is 3 MB. Where do you start?
words.t: First I open a bundle analyzer, like webpack-bundle-analyzer or rollup-plugin-visualizer, to see what takes the most space. Then I split the code by routes, so each page loads only its own code. Heavy parts like charts, editors or maps load lazily, only when needed. I replace big libraries with smaller ones, for example moment with date-fns, and import only the functions I use so tree shaking works. I check for duplicated packages. Finally I add a size budget in CI, so the bundle does not grow again.
a: bundle is 3 MB. Where do you start?

words.w: How does V8 run JavaScript, and why should objects keep the same shape?
words.t: V8 сначала интерпретирует, горячий код компилирует. Быстрый код ждёт одинаковую форму объектов (те же поля, тот же порядок). Иначе деоптимизация.
a: How does V8 run JavaScript, and why should objects keep the same shape
words.ex: V8 turns the code into bytecode and runs it. While it runs, it watches which types it sees. Code that runs often is compiled to fast machine code. This fast code expects objects to look the same every time: same fields, same order. If I add fields in a different order, or change a field from number to string, the fast code is thrown away. So I create objects in one place with all fields, and I do not use delete in hot code.
words.exT: V8 сначала интерпретирует, горячий код компилирует. Быстрый код ждёт одинаковую форму объектов (те же поля, тот же порядок). Иначе деоптимизация.

words.w: How does garbage collection work in V8?
words.t: Молодое поколение чистится часто и дёшево, старое — редко, инкрементально и в фоне. Даже без утечек много аллокаций даёт фризы.
a: How does garbage collection work in V8
words.ex: Most objects die very fast. So V8 keeps new objects in a small young space and cleans it often. This cleaning is cheap. Objects that survive two cleanings move to the old space. The old space is cleaned with mark and sweep. This is done in small steps and partly in background threads, so the page does not freeze. One important point: even without a leak, creating many objects very fast makes the GC work hard, and the user sees small freezes.
words.exT: Молодое поколение чистится часто и дёшево, старое — редко, инкрементально и в фоне. Даже без утечек много аллокаций даёт фризы.

words.w: What are the common memory leaks in a single-page app, and how do you find them?
words.t: Утечки: неснятые слушатели и таймеры, замыкания с большими данными, удалённые DOM-узлы в переменных, растущие кэши. Ищу сравнением heap snapshots.
a: What are the common memory leaks in a single-page app, and how do you find them
words.ex: The usual leaks are simple. An event listener or setInterval that nobody removes. A closure that keeps a big array alive. A DOM node that is removed from the page but still stored in a variable. A cache or a store that grows and never deletes anything. To find them, I open DevTools, take a heap snapshot, repeat the action several times, take another snapshot, and compare. I look at what grew and who holds it. The allocation timeline shows which code creates the objects.
words.exT: Утечки: неснятые слушатели и таймеры, замыкания с большими данными, удалённые DOM-узлы в переменных, растущие кэши. Ищу сравнением heap snapshots.

words.w: WeakMap, WeakSet, WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry — when do you use them?
words.t: WeakMap не удерживает ключи — для метаданных и кэшей по объекту. WeakRef и FinalizationRegistry непредсказуемы, только для необязательных кэшей.
a: WeakMap, WeakSet, WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry — when do you use them
words.ex: A normal Map keeps its keys alive forever. A WeakMap does not: when the key object is gone, the entry is gone too. So I use it to store extra data about an object, for example private data or a cache by object. A WeakRef is a reference that can become empty at any time. A FinalizationRegistry calls a function after an object is collected. We never know when that happens, so I use these two only for caches where losing data is fine.
words.exT: WeakMap не удерживает ключи — для метаданных и кэшей по объекту. WeakRef и FinalizationRegistry непредсказуемы, только для необязательных кэшей.

words.w: structuredClone vs JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) vs spread?
words.t: Spread — поверхностно; JSON теряет undefined, Date, Map, падает на циклах; structuredClone — настоящая глубокая копия, но без функций и DOM, классы становятся объектами.
a: structuredClone vs JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) vs spread
words.ex: Spread is a shallow copy. Nested objects are still shared. The JSON trick is a deep copy but with problems: undefined is removed, a Date becomes a string, Map and Set become empty objects, and a circular reference throws. structuredClone is the right tool for a deep copy. It handles Dates, Maps, Sets and cycles. But it throws on functions and DOM nodes, and class instances become plain objects.
words.exT: Spread — поверхностно; JSON теряет undefined, Date, Map, падает на циклах; structuredClone — настоящая глубокая копия, но без функций и DOM, классы становятся объектами.

words.w: What is the difference between the call stack, the heap and the task queues?
words.t: Стек — текущие функции (переполнение при глубокой рекурсии), куча — объекты (утечка = рост), очереди — колбэки для event loop (долгая задача = фриз).
a: What is the difference between the call stack, the heap and the task queues
words.ex: The call stack is the list of functions that are running now. If recursion goes too deep, the stack overflows. The heap is the memory where objects live; the garbage collector manages it, and a leak means the heap grows. The task queues hold callbacks, for example from setTimeout or promises. The event loop takes them one by one when the stack is empty. A long function on the stack blocks the loop, and the page freezes.
words.exT: Стек — текущие функции (переполнение при глубокой рекурсии), куча — объекты (утечка = рост), очереди — колбэки для event loop (долгая задача = фриз).

words.w: In what order do microtasks, macrotasks, requestAnimationFrame and rendering run?
words.t: Макрозадача → все микрозадачи (и новые тоже) → при кадре rAF и рендер. Бесконечные микрозадачи блокируют отрисовку; setTimeout(0) — следующий оборот.
a: In what order do microtasks, macrotasks, requestAnimationFrame and rendering run
words.ex: The event loop takes one macrotask, for example a click handler. After it, the loop runs every microtask, so all promise callbacks. If a microtask adds another microtask, it also runs now. This is why an endless promise chain freezes the page. Then, if the screen needs a new frame, the browser runs requestAnimationFrame callbacks, calculates layout and paints. setTimeout with zero delay is a new macrotask, so it runs after the paint may already have happened.
words.exT: Макрозадача → все микрозадачи (и новые тоже) → при кадре rAF и рендер. Бесконечные микрозадачи блокируют отрисовку; setTimeout(0) — следующий оборот.

words.w: What does async/await become after compilation, and how much does await cost?
words.t: Async-функция — машина состояний на промисах; await стоит один microtask; код после await всегда позже; внутри try/catch нужен return await.
a: What does async/await become after compilation, and how much does await cost
words.ex: An async function is split into steps. Each await is a point where the function stops and later continues from a promise callback. Since 2019, await on a native promise costs one microtask. Even `await 42` goes to the microtask queue. So the code after await always runs later, not right now. This matters for tests that check order, and for try/catch: inside a try block I must write `return await`, otherwise the catch does not see the error.
words.exT: Async-функция — машина состояний на промисах; await стоит один microtask; код после await всегда позже; внутри try/catch нужен return await.

words.w: How do you cancel an async operation in JavaScript?
words.t: Промисы не отменяются. AbortController: signal в fetch и свои функции, проверка между шагами, abort в cleanup эффекта. AbortSignal.timeout/any для комбинаций.
a: How do you cancel an async operation in JavaScript
words.ex: A promise has no cancel method. The standard tool is AbortController. I create a controller and pass controller.signal to fetch, to addEventListener and to my own async functions. Inside them I check signal.aborted between steps or stop when the abort event fires. In React I create the controller inside useEffect and call abort in the cleanup function. This also fixes the problem when an old request finishes after a new one. AbortSignal.timeout and AbortSignal.any help to combine a timeout with user cancel.
words.exT: Промисы не отменяются. AbortController: signal в fetch и свои функции, проверка между шагами, abort в cleanup эффекта. AbortSignal.timeout/any для комбинаций.

words.w: What is an unhandled rejection, and how do you handle errors globally in the browser?
words.t: Промис отклонён без catch → unhandledrejection; плюс window.onerror и error boundaries, отправка в мониторинг. Ошибки в хендлерах и async до boundary не доходят.
a: What is an unhandled rejection, and how do you handle errors globally in the browser
words.ex: If a promise rejects and no catch is attached before the microtask queue is empty, the browser fires the unhandledrejection event. I listen to it and to window.onerror for normal errors. I send them to a service like Sentry with the user id and the app version, and I show a simple fallback. Render errors in React go to error boundaries. But errors in event handlers and in async code do not reach boundaries, so the global handlers are the safety net.
words.exT: Промис отклонён без catch → unhandledrejection; плюс window.onerror и error boundaries, отправка в мониторинг. Ошибки в хендлерах и async до boundary не доходят.

words.w: Async iterators and generators — where are they useful on the frontend?
words.t: Асинхронные генераторы — данные со временем: стримы, SSE, страницы API. for await даёт back-pressure, остановка через break.
a: Async iterators and generators — where are they useful on the frontend
words.ex: An async generator is a function that gives values one by one, and each value can arrive later. I use it to read a fetch body as a stream, to consume server-sent events, or to walk through API pages. The consumer uses for await. It asks for the next value only when it is ready, so the producer does not run ahead. To stop, I just break out of the loop. The logic is also easy to test without React.
words.exT: Асинхронные генераторы — данные со временем: стримы, SSE, страницы API. for await даёт back-pressure, остановка через break.

words.w: Web Workers — what would you move there, and how?
words.t: В воркер — тяжёлые вычисления без DOM. Общение через postMessage, ArrayBuffer передавать без копии, Comlink для удобства. Service worker — другое, это сетевой прокси.
a: Web Workers — what would you move there, and how
words.ex: A worker is a second thread. It cannot touch the DOM, but it can do heavy work while the page stays smooth. Good candidates are parsing a big JSON or CSV, building a search index, compressing or resizing images. The page and the worker talk with postMessage. For big data I transfer the ArrayBuffer instead of copying it. A library like Comlink makes worker calls look like normal async functions. A service worker is different: it is a network proxy, not a place for computations.
words.exT: В воркер — тяжёлые вычисления без DOM. Общение через postMessage, ArrayBuffer передавать без копии, Comlink для удобства. Service worker — другое, это сетевой прокси.

words.w: How do you implement retry with exponential backoff correctly?
words.t: Ретраить только безопасные запросы и ретраибельные ошибки (сеть, 429, 5xx). Задержка растёт с джиттером, лимит попыток, Retry-After, стоп по signal, idempotency key для POST.
a: How do you implement retry with exponential backoff correctly
words.ex: First I check that the request is safe to repeat. A GET is safe. A POST is safe only if it has an idempotency key. Then I check the error: network errors, 429 and 5xx can be retried; 400 or 401 cannot. The delay grows, for example 1, 2, 4 seconds, with a random part so that many clients do not retry at the same moment. If the server sends a Retry-After header, I use that value. I stop after a few tries, and I also stop if the AbortSignal fires.
words.exT: Ретраить только безопасные запросы и ретраибельные ошибки (сеть, 429, 5xx). Задержка растёт с джиттером, лимит попыток, Retry-After, стоп по signal, idempotency key для POST.

words.w: setTimeout, setInterval, requestAnimationFrame, requestIdleCallback — what is the difference?
words.t: setTimeout — минимальная задержка; setInterval накапливается; rAF — перед кадром, для анимаций и измерений; rIC — в простое, для неприоритетного.
a: setTimeout, setInterval, requestAnimationFrame, requestIdleCallback — what is the difference
words.ex: setTimeout gives a minimum delay, not an exact one, and background tabs slow it down. setInterval keeps firing even if the previous callback is still slow, so I usually use setTimeout that calls itself. requestAnimationFrame runs right before the browser paints and stops in hidden tabs. It is the right place for animations and for reading layout. requestIdleCallback runs when the browser has nothing else to do, so it is good for low-priority work like analytics, and it gives a deadline I must respect.
words.exT: setTimeout — минимальная задержка; setInterval накапливается; rAF — перед кадром, для анимаций и измерений; rIC — в простое, для неприоритетного.

words.w: How does fetch streaming work, and when would you use it?
words.t: response.body — ReadableStream: читаю чанки, декодирую TextDecoder, показываю сразу (стриминг ответа ИИ, большие выгрузки); отмена через signal.
a: How does fetch streaming work, and when would you use it
words.ex: Normally I call response.json() and wait for the whole body. With streaming I take response.body.getReader() and read small chunks as they come. I decode them with a TextDecoder in stream mode and show the text right away. This is how chat apps show AI answers word by word. It also lets me start rendering a big list before the download ends. The abort signal cancels the stream. When I split the text by lines, I must keep the last incomplete piece for the next chunk.
words.exT: response.body — ReadableStream: читаю чанки, декодирую TextDecoder, показываю сразу (стриминг ответа ИИ, большие выгрузки); отмена через signal.

words.w: What is a closure, how does it work in memory, and where does it cause bugs?
words.t: Замыкание — функция плюс переменные вокруг неё; они живут, пока жива функция. Используется везде: приватные переменные, debounce, хуки. Баги: старые значения в колбэках, var в циклах, утечки памяти.
a: What is a closure, how does it work in memory, and where does it cause bugs
words.ex: A closure is a function plus the variables around it. When I create a function inside another function, the inner function remembers the outer variables. It keeps them even after the outer function has returned. The engine does not copy the values; it keeps the real variables alive in memory while the inner function exists. I use closures every day: a counter with a private variable, debounce, event handlers, and every React hook. The typical bugs: a callback uses an old value because it was created in an old render; a for loop with var gives the same i to every callback; and a closure that holds a big array keeps it in memory for too long.
words.exT: Замыкание — функция плюс переменные вокруг неё; они живут, пока жива функция. Используется везде: приватные переменные, debounce, хуки. Баги: старые значения в колбэках, var в циклах, утечки памяти.

words.w: How does lexical scope work, and what is the scope chain?
words.t: Область видимости определяется местом в коде, а не вызовом. Поиск переменной идёт по цепочке наружу до глобальной. Цепочка фиксируется при создании функции — отсюда замыкания. Исключение — this.
a: How does lexical scope work, and what is the scope chain
words.ex: JavaScript has lexical scope. This means the engine decides which variables a function can see by looking at where the function is written in the code. Each function creates a new scope, and blocks with let and const create block scopes. When the code reads a variable, the engine looks in the current scope first. If it is not there, it looks in the outer scope, and so on up to the global scope. This chain is fixed when the function is created, and that is exactly what makes closures possible. The only exception is this, which depends on how the function is called, not where it is written.
words.exT: Область видимости определяется местом в коде, а не вызовом. Поиск переменной идёт по цепочке наружу до глобальной. Цепочка фиксируется при создании функции — отсюда замыкания. Исключение — this.

words.w: What is the iterable protocol, and why does spread work on a Map but not on a plain object?
words.t: Итерируемое = есть Symbol.iterator, который возвращает объект с next(). Map/Set/массивы — да, объект — нет; поэтому [...obj] падает, а {...obj} работает через ключи.
a: What is the iterable protocol, and why does spread work on a Map but not on a plain object
words.ex: for-of, array spread, Array.from and destructuring all use one protocol. They call the Symbol.iterator method and then call next() until done is true. Map, Set, arrays and strings have this method. A plain object does not, so [...obj] throws. But {...obj} works, because object spread does not use the protocol; it just copies own keys. I can make my own class iterable by adding a generator method named Symbol.iterator.
words.exT: Итерируемое = есть Symbol.iterator, который возвращает объект с next(). Map/Set/массивы — да, объект — нет; поэтому [...obj] падает, а {...obj} работает через ключи.

words.w: What are Proxy and Reflect, and which libraries use them?
words.t: Proxy перехватывает операции с объектом, Reflect делает стандартное действие. На этом стоят Vue 3, MobX, Immer. Минусы — скорость и нет полифила.
a: What are Proxy and Reflect, and which libraries use them
words.ex: A Proxy sits between the code and the object. When the code reads a field, the Proxy's get trap runs; when it writes, the set trap runs. Reflect.get and Reflect.set do the normal operation, so a trap can do its work and then call the default. Vue 3 uses the get trap to remember which component read a field, and the set trap to update that component. Immer uses a Proxy to record changes and then builds a new immutable object. The cost is speed in hot code, and a Proxy cannot be polyfilled.
words.exT: Proxy перехватывает операции с объектом, Reflect делает стандартное действие. На этом стоят Vue 3, MobX, Immer. Минусы — скорость и нет полифила.

words.w: What are Symbols for, besides unique keys?
words.t: Символы — уникальные ключи, невидимые для JSON и keys; well-known символы — хуки языка (iterator, toPrimitive, hasInstance); Symbol.for — общий символ по имени.
a: What are Symbols for, besides unique keys
words.ex: A symbol is a unique key that JSON.stringify and Object.keys skip. The well-known symbols are hooks into the language. Symbol.iterator makes an object work with for-of. Symbol.toPrimitive controls what happens when the object is turned into a string or a number. Symbol.hasInstance customizes instanceof. Symbol.for('name') returns the same symbol everywhere, even across iframes. React uses it for the $$typeof field on elements, so that an element from JSON cannot be injected.
words.exT: Символы — уникальные ключи, невидимые для JSON и keys; well-known символы — хуки языка (iterator, toPrimitive, hasInstance); Symbol.for — общий символ по имени.

words.w: How do ES modules differ from CommonJS at runtime?
words.t: ESM — статическая линковка, живые привязки, асинхронно; CJS — синхронный require, копия значения. Смесь даёт default undefined; tree shaking работает только с ESM.
a: How do ES modules differ from CommonJS at runtime
words.ex: With ES modules the browser or bundler first reads all import and export statements, builds the graph and links everything. Only then the code runs. An import is a live link: if the exported value changes, the importer sees the change. Top-level await is possible. CommonJS is different: require is a normal function call that runs the file right now and returns module.exports as it is at that moment. When tools mix the two, a CommonJS module shows up as an object with a default field, and that is where "default is undefined" comes from. Tree shaking needs the static ES module graph.
words.exT: ESM — статическая линковка, живые привязки, асинхронно; CJS — синхронный require, копия значения. Смесь даёт default undefined; tree shaking работает только с ESM.

words.w: How do class fields, private fields and arrow methods work with this?
words.t: Поля создаются до тела конструктора; #private — настоящая приватность; стрелочное поле держит this, но копируется на каждый экземпляр и не переопределяется через прототип.
a: How do class fields, private fields and arrow methods work with this
words.ex: Field initializers run for every new instance, in order, before the constructor body, and this is already set. A field with # is private: no code outside the class can read it, and `#x in obj` checks if an object has it. An arrow function as a field captures this, so I can pass it as a callback safely. The price: every instance holds its own function, and a subclass cannot override it on the prototype. Normal methods are shared through the prototype and lose this when passed as callbacks.
words.exT: Поля создаются до тела конструктора; #private — настоящая приватность; стрелочное поле держит this, но копируется на каждый экземпляр и не переопределяется через прототип.

words.w: What is prototype pollution, and how do you protect against it?
words.t: Deep merge чужого JSON с ключом __proto__ меняет Object.prototype. Защита: блокировать __proto__/constructor/prototype, Map или null-прототип, обновлять библиотеки.
a: What is prototype pollution, and how do you protect against it
words.ex: Imagine a deep merge function that copies user JSON into a config object. If the JSON has a key "__proto__", the merge writes to Object.prototype. Now every object in the app has that field, for example isAdmin: true. To protect: the merge and the deep-set helpers must skip the keys __proto__, constructor and prototype. User data is better kept in a Map or in an object created with Object.create(null). And I keep libraries like lodash updated, because they had exactly this bug.
words.exT: Deep merge чужого JSON с ключом __proto__ меняет Object.prototype. Защита: блокировать __proto__/constructor/prototype, Map или null-прототип, обновлять библиотеки.

words.w: Explain property descriptors, getters and setters, and Object.freeze.
words.t: Дескрипторы: writable/enumerable/configurable или get/set. freeze поверхностный. Геттеры дали реактивность до Proxy; non-enumerable скрывает поле от JSON и spread.
a: Explain property descriptors, getters and setters, and Object.freeze
words.ex: Object.defineProperty lets me set the flags of a property. writable means it can change, enumerable means it shows up in loops and in spread, configurable means it can be deleted or changed again. A property can also be a pair of get and set functions. Object.freeze turns off writable and configurable for all own properties, but nested objects are not frozen, so a deep freeze needs recursion. Vue 2 and MobX used getters and setters to watch changes before Proxy existed. A non-enumerable property is a way to hide a helper field from JSON and spread.
words.exT: Дескрипторы: writable/enumerable/configurable или get/set. freeze поверхностный. Геттеры дали реактивность до Proxy; non-enumerable скрывает поле от JSON и spread.

words.w: Conditional types with infer — how do you get a function's return type or a promise's value?
words.t: infer — переменная типа внутри extends; так написаны ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited. Условный тип применяется к каждому члену union; обернуть в кортеж, чтобы выключить.
a: Conditional types with infer — how do you get a function's return type or a promise's value
words.ex: infer declares a type variable inside the extends check, and TypeScript finds its value. This is how ReturnType, Parameters and Awaited are written. When the type parameter is a union, TypeScript applies the conditional type to each member separately, so Unwrap<A | B> becomes Unwrap<A> | Unwrap<B>. Usually this is what I want. If not, I wrap both sides in a tuple: [T] extends [X].
words.exT: infer — переменная типа внутри extends; так написаны ReturnType, Parameters, Awaited. Условный тип применяется к каждому члену union; обернуть в кортеж, чтобы выключить.

words.w: Mapped types and template literal types — give a practical example.
words.t: Mapped type — цикл по ключам, as переименовывает/фильтрует; шаблонные литералы строят имена: onNameChange из name, типизированные параметры роута из пути.
a: Mapped types and template literal types — give a practical example
words.ex: A mapped type is a loop over keys: { [K in keyof T]: ... }. With the as clause I can change the key name or drop some keys. Template literal types build strings at the type level. Together they let me take a props type and produce an event handlers type, for example onNameChange for the field name. Another example is typed route params from a path like "/users/:id". The compiler then catches renames for free.
words.exT: Mapped type — цикл по ключам, as переименовывает/фильтрует; шаблонные литералы строят имена: onNameChange из name, типизированные параметры роута из пути.

words.w: What is structural typing, and when does it cause problems?
words.t: Типы сравниваются по форме, не по имени: UserId и OrderId как string можно перепутать. Решение — брендированные типы; проверка лишних полей только для литералов.
a: What is structural typing, and when does it cause problems
words.ex: In TypeScript, if two types have the same fields, they are compatible. This is flexible, but it has a downside: two different IDs that are both strings can be swapped and nothing complains. The fix is a branded type: type UserId = string & { __brand: 'UserId' } and a small function that creates it. Another surprise: extra properties are checked only when you write an object literal directly, not when you pass a variable.
words.exT: Типы сравниваются по форме, не по имени: UserId и OrderId как string можно перепутать. Решение — брендированные типы; проверка лишних полей только для литералов.

words.w: Why can you pass Array<Dog> where Array<Animal> is expected, and why is that unsafe?
words.t: Массивы ковариантны ради удобства, для мутабельных это небезопасно. Параметры функций проверяются наоборот (strictFunctionTypes), но не для методов.
a: Why can you pass Array<Dog> where Array<Animal> is expected, and why is that unsafe
words.ex: If Dog is an Animal, TypeScript also says Array<Dog> is an Array<Animal>. For reading this is fine. For writing it is not: through the Animal-typed reference I can push a Cat into the Dog array. TypeScript allows this on purpose, because the strict version would be very annoying. Function parameters work in the opposite direction: a function that accepts Animal can be used where a function that accepts Dog is expected. strictFunctionTypes enforces this for function types, but not for methods.
words.exT: Массивы ковариантны ради удобства, для мутабельных это небезопасно. Параметры функций проверяются наоборот (strictFunctionTypes), но не для методов.

words.w: satisfies vs a type annotation vs as const — when do you use each?
words.t: Аннотация расширяет тип; satisfies проверяет, но сохраняет точный вывод; as const сужает литералы. Для таблиц констант — as const satisfies T.
a: satisfies vs a type annotation vs as const — when do you use each
words.ex: If I write const routes: Record<string, Route> = {...}, TypeScript forgets the real keys, so routes.home is just a Route and may not exist. With satisfies Record<string, Route>, the object is checked, but its exact keys stay known. as const makes values exact: 'GET' stays the literal 'GET', arrays become readonly tuples. For tables of constants I use both together: as const satisfies T.
words.exT: Аннотация расширяет тип; satisfies проверяет, но сохраняет точный вывод; as const сужает литералы. Для таблиц констант — as const satisfies T.

words.w: How do you make a switch over a union exhaustive, and why does never help?
words.t: В default передаю значение в assertNever(x: never). Новый вариант union ломает компиляцию ровно там, где не обработан.
a: How do you make a switch over a union exhaustive, and why does never help
words.ex: I write a small helper: function assertNever(x: never): never. In the default case of the switch I call it with the value. If all cases are handled, the value's type at that point is never, so it compiles. When a new variant is added to the union and not handled, the type is no longer never, and the build fails exactly at the switch that needs a new case. This is a cheap safety net for reducers and status rendering.
words.exT: В default передаю значение в assertNever(x: never). Новый вариант union ломает компиляцию ровно там, где не обработан.

words.w: Enums vs a union of string literals vs an as const object?
words.t: Предпочитаю union литералов или as const объект: ноль рантайма, работает со всеми сборщиками. Числовые enum небезопасны, const enum ломается на границах модулей и в esbuild.
a: Enums vs a union of string literals vs an as const object
words.ex: A union of string literals is only a type, so it costs nothing at runtime. When I also need the values in code, I write an object with as const and derive the type with typeof Obj[keyof typeof Obj]. TypeScript enums generate real objects. Numeric enums accept any number, which is unsafe. const enum is inlined by tsc but not by esbuild or Babel, and it does not work across package boundaries. Many teams simply forbid enums.
words.exT: Предпочитаю union литералов или as const объект: ноль рантайма, работает со всеми сборщиками. Числовые enum небезопасны, const enum ломается на границах модулей и в esbuild.

words.w: Which strict flags matter most, and what does noUncheckedIndexedAccess change?
words.t: strict — база; noUncheckedIndexedAccess делает индекс T | undefined; exactOptionalPropertyTypes отличает отсутствие поля от undefined; verbatimModuleSyntax требует import type.
a: Which strict flags matter most, and what does noUncheckedIndexedAccess change
words.ex: strict turns on null checks, no implicit any, strict function types and a few more. noUncheckedIndexedAccess says: an index access may give undefined, so handle it. It catches real bugs in loops and lookups, but adds some noise. exactOptionalPropertyTypes makes { a?: T } different from { a: T | undefined }. verbatimModuleSyntax forces me to write import type for types, so bundlers can drop those imports without running the type checker.
words.exT: strict — база; noUncheckedIndexedAccess делает индекс T | undefined; exactOptionalPropertyTypes отличает отсутствие поля от undefined; verbatimModuleSyntax требует import type.

words.w: How do you type a generic React component, and what is the problem with forwardRef?
words.t: Дженерик-компонент — дженерик-функция, T выводится из пропсов. forwardRef теряет дженерик (нужен каст); в React 19 ref — обычный проп.
a: How do you type a generic React component, and what is the problem with forwardRef
words.ex: A generic component is just a generic function. When I write <Table rows={users} />, TypeScript infers T from the rows prop, and the render callbacks are typed. forwardRef returns a non-generic type, so the generic is lost. The old workaround was a cast or a module declaration. In React 19 function components receive ref as a normal prop, so forwardRef is not needed. For components with an as prop I use the ComponentPropsWithoutRef pattern.
words.exT: Дженерик-компонент — дженерик-функция, T выводится из пропсов. forwardRef теряет дженерик (нужен каст); в React 19 ref — обычный проп.

words.w: Where does TypeScript stop protecting you at runtime, and what do you do about it?
words.t: Типы исчезают в рантайме; сеть, storage, URL, JSON.parse — unknown. Валидирую на границе через zod/valibot и беру тип из схемы.
a: Where does TypeScript stop protecting you at runtime, and what do you do about it
words.ex: Everything that comes from outside is unknown at runtime: API responses, localStorage, query strings, messages from iframes. A cast like as User only makes the compiler quiet; it does not check anything. So I describe the data once with a zod or valibot schema, parse it at the boundary, and use z.infer to get the TypeScript type from the same schema. Then the type and the check can never disagree. In forms the same schema gives validation messages.
words.exT: Типы исчезают в рантайме; сеть, storage, URL, JSON.parse — unknown. Валидирую на границе через zod/valibot и беру тип из схемы.

words.w: What happens between setState and the change on the screen?
words.t: setState → апдейт с приоритетом → render-фаза строит новое дерево (может прерываться) → commit синхронно меняет DOM → layout-эффекты → paint → useEffect.
a: What happens between setState and the change on the screen
words.ex: When I call setState, React stores the update on that component with a priority and schedules work. In the render phase React calls the component functions, compares the result with the current tree and collects the changes. With concurrent features this phase can pause and continue later. The commit phase is synchronous: React changes the DOM, runs useLayoutEffect and ref callbacks. Then the browser paints. After that React runs useEffect callbacks. This is why render must have no side effects, and why layout effects block the paint.
words.exT: setState → апдейт с приоритетом → render-фаза строит новое дерево (может прерываться) → commit синхронно меняет DOM → layout-эффекты → paint → useEffect.

words.w: What problem does concurrent rendering solve, and what are lanes?
words.t: Конкурентный рендер прерывает тяжёлые обновления ради срочного ввода. Lanes — уровни приоритета. useTransition помечает обновление как неприоритетное; рендер должен быть чистым.
a: What problem does concurrent rendering solve, and what are lanes
words.ex: Before React 18, a big update blocked the main thread until it was done. With concurrent rendering React works for a few milliseconds, then checks if there is more urgent work, for example a key press, and handles it first. It can continue the big render later or start it again. Lanes are the priorities: user input is urgent, a transition is low priority, idle work is lowest. useTransition marks an update as low priority, so a heavy list does not delay the key press that caused it. The rule for us: render must be pure, because it may run more than once.
words.exT: Конкурентный рендер прерывает тяжёлые обновления ради срочного ввода. Lanes — уровни приоритета. useTransition помечает обновление как неприоритетное; рендер должен быть чистым.

words.w: useTransition vs useDeferredValue vs debouncing — when do you use each?
words.t: useTransition — когда сам вызываю setState; useDeferredValue — для входящего значения. Оба про рендер; сетевые запросы требуют debounce и отмены.
a: useTransition vs useDeferredValue vs debouncing — when do you use each
words.ex: With useTransition I wrap my own setState call. The input updates right away, and the heavy list updates in the background. I also get isPending to show a spinner. useDeferredValue is for a value I do not control, for example a prop: React gives me a copy that updates when it has time. Both only help with rendering cost. If the cost is network requests, I still need debounce or request cancellation. Often I use both together.
words.exT: useTransition — когда сам вызываю setState; useDeferredValue — для входящего значения. Оба про рендер; сетевые запросы требуют debounce и отмены.

words.w: Why does StrictMode run components and effects twice in development?
words.t: StrictMode дважды вызывает рендер и эффекты (setup→cleanup→setup), чтобы показать нечистый рендер и эффекты без cleanup до того, как они сломаются в конкурентном режиме.
a: Why does StrictMode run components and effects twice in development
words.ex: In development StrictMode calls each component function two times and runs each effect as setup, then cleanup, then setup again. The double render shows side effects inside render, for example an API call or a ref change. The double effect shows subscriptions and timers that have no cleanup. These bugs would also appear when React keeps state during Fast Refresh or in future features. The fix is to make effects safe to run twice, not to remove StrictMode.
words.exT: StrictMode дважды вызывает рендер и эффекты (setup→cleanup→setup), чтобы показать нечистый рендер и эффекты без cleanup до того, как они сломаются в конкурентном режиме.

words.w: How does Suspense work under the hood?
words.t: Компонент бросает промис, ближайший Suspense ловит и показывает fallback; после resolve рендер повторяется, источник данных должен отдать результат из кэша, иначе бесконечный suspend.
a: How does Suspense work under the hood
words.ex: Suspense is built on throwing. When data is not ready, the component throws a promise-like object. React goes up to the nearest Suspense, shows the fallback and waits for the promise. When it resolves, React tries to render the component again. This time the data source must return the value right away from a cache. If it starts a new request again, the component suspends forever. That is why a plain fetch inside a component does not work, and why libraries like TanStack Query or the React 19 use hook with a stable promise are needed.
words.exT: Компонент бросает промис, ближайший Suspense ловит и показывает fallback; после resolve рендер повторяется, источник данных должен отдать результат из кэша, иначе бесконечный suspend.

words.w: How does React decide to keep or recreate a component during reconciliation?
words.t: Переиспользует при том же типе и позиции (и key в списке); иначе размонтирует вместе со стейтом. Смена key сбрасывает форму; компонент внутри компонента — новый тип каждый рендер.
a: How does React decide to keep or recreate a component during reconciliation
words.ex: React compares the new tree with the old one, child by child, by position and type. This makes the algorithm fast. If the type changes, for example a div becomes a span, React removes the whole subtree and creates a new one. If the key changes, the old instance is unmounted and a new one is mounted. I use this on purpose: changing the key of a form resets it. A common bug: a component defined inside another component is a new type on every render, so its state resets every time.
words.exT: Переиспользует при том же типе и позиции (и key в списке); иначе размонтирует вместе со стейтом. Смена key сбрасывает форму; компонент внутри компонента — новый тип каждый рендер.

words.w: What is tearing, and how does useSyncExternalStore prevent it?
words.t: Tearing — в одном рендере две версии внешнего стора из-за паузы. useSyncExternalStore сравнивает снимок и форсирует синхронный рендер; его используют Redux, Zustand.
a: What is tearing, and how does useSyncExternalStore prevent it
words.ex: With concurrent rendering a render can pause in the middle. If an external store, for example Redux, changes during the pause, components rendered later read the new value while earlier ones have the old value. For one frame the UI is inconsistent. useSyncExternalStore subscribes to the store and takes a snapshot. If the snapshot changed during render, React drops the result and renders again synchronously. Redux, Zustand and routers use this hook. It also has getServerSnapshot for SSR.
words.exT: Tearing — в одном рендере две версии внешнего стора из-за паузы. useSyncExternalStore сравнивает снимок и форсирует синхронный рендер; его используют Redux, Zustand.

words.w: Why does a click inside a portal reach a React parent that is not its DOM parent?
words.t: Синтетические события всплывают по дереву React, а не DOM; портал остаётся ребёнком в React, поэтому родитель получает клики. Для click-outside нужна DOM-проверка.
a: Why does a click inside a portal reach a React parent that is not its DOM parent
words.ex: React adds one native listener per event type on the root. When an event happens, React walks its own component tree, not the DOM tree. A modal rendered with createPortal into document.body is still a child of its React parent. So the parent's onClick sees clicks inside the modal, and context also works. The downside: a "click outside" check cannot use React propagation. It must check the DOM with element.contains or use a native listener.
words.exT: Синтетические события всплывают по дереву React, а не DOM; портал остаётся ребёнком в React, поэтому родитель получает клики. Для click-outside нужна DOM-проверка.

words.w: What is automatic batching in React 18, and what does flushSync do?
